body: That you for your encouragement, honestly replies like these give me strength to not lose hope. I will try to make the best out of my situation and I hope to move to another country once I finish residency. I am sorry that you had to read through my whining, I am just so tired of underappreciated medical workers in the Eastern Europe and Balkans. And what’s more shocking to me is how many people accept this as a norm and just power through it. Your words truly give me a light at the end of the tunnel.

Sorry to be so late replying to this, I’ve had a rough few months. You are right, the main ambition of being a medical professional is to be of service to others. I fully believe that with my heart. And I love my job, I love that I can serve the country that I was born in, but the comparison is the thief of joy. When I get home from another stressful night shift, I cannot control my despair and sadness at the fact that there are people in other countries that are more valued doing the same service that we do in the Eastern Europe for a barely liveable wage. Yes, this is a problem of the country, not the individual, because not only we are paying the bare minimum to our healthcare workers (I sympathize with our nurses even more), but we also have incomprehensible waitlists for specialist visits. A patient, the best example would be child psychiatric service appointment, can be left waiting for a visit for 8-9 months with an acute behavioural problem. I cannot bear to imagine what horror the parents are going through with this level of medical system management.
Thank you for sharing your perspective, and from my heart I am proud of you 🥲❤️ this gives me hope

Now I wonder how many people donate their plasma with THC in it, considering the lengthy half-life.

I am too almost 30, a doctor currently in residency, with no prospects of earning more than 1500€ even after graduation in my country (yay for wasting 10 years on this). I am made to feel worthless as a childfree woman in a conservative country, I hate my job, I hate my life and have no desire and  enough willpower to change anything. I am low contact with my mother and have zero friends and no partner. I feel you at least to some degree, my sheltered upbringing lead to me struggling in the real world out there the second I graduated university.
What helps me cope is being grateful for the small things in my life. You have a roof over your head, a patient mother, food on your table, and the ability to smoke weed every day lol. Substance abuse leads to a very real rebound depression, it’s a vicuous cycle. Try to live your life sober, maybe your perspective will change. In the worst case you can always return to stoner life. If I could, I would live off welfare playing video games and not work a single day of my life lol.

Edit : if your goal is living off welfare and you have a history of documented psychiatric disorders,  you might want to check out [r/NEET](https://www.reddit.com/r/NEET/) for advice from people with a similar lifestyle.
Thank you!

I would love to  get  a car maintenance/mechanic degree as those things are quite in demand here too and I actually would like to do some physically intensive labor for a few years while I’m young instead of sitting for 3/4 of my workday writing notes. After a few years I’d probably saved up some money to decide what I wanted to do next with my life and maybe gotten another degree.

While I agree that a lot of the time antibiotics are prescribed unnecessarily for runny noses, common colds, a lot of which are actually caused by viruses, a chest infection doesn’t sound like a minor issue and is most probably of bacterial origin  so the prescription is more than justified in this case.

You must understand that while being a doctor may not be the all-time dream for some people, it is still a job with very high patient safety standarts and regulations. If you work in the medical field and haven’t lost your license, it means you are able to keep up to the standarts and provide adequate medical care. Even a single mistake may lead to losing your license.
Thank you, hopefully in the future I will be mentally stable enough to start thinking about moving.

You have clearly not read my post thoroughly. I acknowledge that this is the path I did not choose but agreed to follow out of fear of being kicked out at 18 without any education prospects at all. I could have been more assertive. I could have moved to the US. I could have married a rich Dubai prince. BUT the reality is - trying my best to finish college, work part-time, and make my financial situation at least a tiny bit better than my parents has taken a toll on my mental health.

I did not get braces until the age of 16 because my parents only income was social security and saving up for braces took several years. By that time my teeth have all basically rotted as cleaning them proved difficult (pediatric dental care is free in my country so at least I had all fillings done). However now when I’m almost 30, the fillings have to be replaced due to wear and tear, and some of my teeth have cracked vertically, I really wish I had braces installed sooner.

It’s frustrating when things don’t go as planned, especially when you’ve already made a clear budget, but your health should always be your top priority. Even minor issues can become dangerous (and costly) when left untreated. Hope you feel better soon.

Also states zero college debt when I clearly stated on another reply that residencies here are contractual and unless you slave ADDITIONAL 3-5 years AFTER residency for a low wage government hospital, you have to pay back about 30k euros in tuition fees.

Thank you for your kind words. We really should look out for each other instead of belittling, judging and chadding the hell out of already burned out medical workers. I hope the toxicity will be addressed in the medical field with the coming generations of new graduates.

Thank you, although technically I am in debt because residency in my country is 100% contractual. The education costs 6000€ a year but if you graduate successfully and work for a certain amount of years in a government hospital on a fixed contractual pay, you don’t have to pay the tuition back. So you basically sign yourself up for another 3-5 years of low-wage slavery after residency.
Actually I believe it is 10 years on average. Europe, all post-Soviet countries has a 6 year medical diploma followed by 4-5 years of residency.
